x: Install Mnemo, then make your first note, mind map and deck.

Grab the build for your computer from the download page . There's no account to make, and your library stays on your own machine. Windows Run the .exe installer. It's made for Windows 10 and 11. The build isn't signed yet, so Windows may show a SmartScreen warning the first time. Click More info , then Run anyway . Mnemo needs the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime. Almost every Windows 10 and 11 machine has it already. If the app won't start, install WebView2 and try again. macOS Open the .pkg installer. It runs on Apple silicon Macs, M1 and newer. There's no build for Intel Macs. Linux Use the AppImage for most distros, or the portable .tar.gz if you'd rather unpack it yourself. The build targets Ubuntu 22.04 and newer. Give the AppImage permission to run from its file properties, or with chmod +x on the file. It also needs a few system libraries. On Ubuntu 24.04 this installs them all: sudo apt install libfuse2t64 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libjavascriptcoregtk-4.1-0 libgtk-3-0t64 libnotify4 Package names differ a little on other distros. First launch A short setup asks for your name and language, and then you're in. Mnemo checks for updates on its own and asks before installing one. Mnemo is still young and moving fast. Keep a backup of your library, especially before you update.

Press Ctrl N , give it a title and start typing. Notes save on their own as you write. Type / at the start of a line to pick a block, like a heading, a list or a table. Or just type Markdown: # and a space makes a heading, - makes a list. There's more in Notes .

Open Mind maps , choose New , then Map . Press N and click to place your first node, and name it after the subject. With a node selected, Tab adds a child and Enter adds a sibling, so you can build the whole map without touching the mouse. There's more in Mind maps .

Open Flashcards , make a new deck and add a few cards from something you're studying right now. Keep each card to one question. Ctrl Enter saves a card and keeps the editor open for the next one. Then press Study . Try to recall the answer, reveal it and grade how it went. Mnemo uses that grade to decide when you'll see the card again. When the session ends, you're done for today. Missed a day? No problem, due cards simply wait for you. There's more in Flashcards .

These few save the most time. On a Mac, use Cmd wherever you see Ctrl . Ctrl K Open the command palette to jump to any note, deck or action Ctrl N New note / Pick a block type in a note Ctrl P Find a note by title Alt Enter Open the focused note in the side peek, next to what you're working on Tab and Enter Add a child or sibling node in a mind map Ctrl Enter Save a card and start the next Space Reveal the answer in a review, press again for Good 1 to 4 Grade Again, Hard, Good or Easy In the command palette, start with > to see only actions, or # to search deck tags. Most shortcuts can be changed under Settings , then Keyboard .
Jump to any note, deck or action, and keep a second note open beside you.

Press Ctrl K anywhere, or click Search at the top of the app. It finds note titles, deck names, pages and actions like toggling the theme or the sidebar. With nothing typed, it shows what you opened recently. Start with > to see only actions. Start with # to search deck tags. Use the arrow keys and Enter to open a result, and Esc to close. The palette doesn't search inside notes or cards. For those, read on.

Ctrl P Find a note by title in the sidebar Ctrl F Find and replace inside the note you're reading, with case and whole word options Index The floating list of a note's headings. Click one to jump there. To search the text of your cards, use Browse cards in Flashcards .

The side peek keeps a note or card open beside whatever you're working on, so you can read one thing while writing another. Hold Alt and click a note in the sidebar. Focus a note and press Alt Enter . Choose Open in side peek from a note's menu, or from a card's menu in Browse cards. Notes in the side peek are for reading. Open full takes the note to the main view so you can edit it. Links to other notes open right there in the peek. The peek can float over your work or dock to the left or right. Drag its inner edge to resize it. Esc closes it, unless you've pinned or docked it.
Write in blocks, format as you type and keep everything tidy.

Every line in a note is a block. Type / at the start of a line and keep typing to filter the menu. The English block names work in every language. Text and headings Paragraphs and four levels of headings. Headings also show up in the note's index, so you can jump around long notes. Lists and to dos Bullet lists, numbered lists and checklists. Quote, callout and warning Asides that stand out from the text. Click a callout's icon to change its emoji. Code A code block with highlighting for the language you pick. Two columns Two stacks of blocks side by side, with a divider you can drag. Image and table Pictures with an optional caption, and tables with rows and columns. Equation A block of LaTeX maths on its own line. Page A note inside a note, shown as a link with its title. Markdown as you type At the start of a line, type a marker and a space: # to #### for headings, - for a list, 1. for a numbered list, [] for a to do, > for a quote, three backticks for code and --- for a divider.

Select text to bring up the formatting bar, or use the keys below. On a Mac, use Cmd for Ctrl . Ctrl B Ctrl I Ctrl U Bold, italic, underline Ctrl Shift S Strikethrough Ctrl Shift H Highlight Ctrl E Inline code Ctrl Shift L Add or edit a link Ctrl Shift E Insert an equation in the line For maths, write LaTeX between dollar signs, like $E = mc^2$ . If the LaTeX has a mistake, it stays as you typed it so you can fix it.

Drag notes into folders in the sidebar, and drag folders into each other to nest them. Star the notes you open most. They sit in their own section at the top. Ctrl P finds a note by title, and Ctrl F finds and replaces inside the one you're reading. Hold Alt and click a note to open it in the side peek, so you can read one note while writing another. A good rule of thumb: one note per topic. When a section outgrows the page, move it into a note of its own.

Notes save as you type, and Ctrl S saves right away. If a save fails, the corner of the note says so and Mnemo keeps retrying. Prefer saving by hand? Turn off Auto save under Settings , then Editor . Closing a note always saves it.

Pick Export from a note's menu. Markdown gives you plain text any editor can open, though images and column layouts don't come along. A .mnemo package keeps everything exactly as it is. Export as PDF lets you pick the paper size, margins, text size and page numbers. Bringing notes in is covered in Importing .
Grow a map from one idea, mostly from the keyboard.

Open Mind maps , choose New , then Map . Pick a name and a starting template. Press N and click to place your first node. Name it after the subject and keep it broad, since everything else grows from there.

Tab Add a child Enter Add a sibling Shift Tab Move a node out from under its parent F2 Edit the label, or double click the node Ctrl D Duplicate the selection Delete Remove the selection Ctrl 0 Fit the whole map on screen Dragging a node moves its whole branch.

The dock at the bottom of the canvas covers what you place by hand. Each tool goes back to Select after one use. V Select Select, drag and resize N Node Place a node and start typing S Shape Place a shape T Text Place a loose label C Connect Draw a link between two nodes F Frame Draw a frame around a group I Image Place a picture To link two branches, press C and drag from one node to the other. Drag the same link again to remove it. Hold Q for a radial menu with the most common actions. When a branch gets crowded, move it into a map of its own.
Export on the map toolbar saves a PNG or SVG picture, or a Markdown outline of the whole map. To move maps between computers, use Transfer in the library to export or import .mnemo packages.
Write cards that stick, study them and let FSRS plan your reviews.
A deck holds cards that belong together, usually one subject or course. A few broad decks work better than lots of tiny ones. Tags handle the finer sorting and turn into filters in the deck view.

One fact per card. If an answer has three parts, make three cards. Ask a real question, something you can try to answer before you flip. Use your own words. Copied sentences test recognition, your own phrasing tests recall. Card types Basic A front and a back. Basic and reverse The same two sides, asked both ways. Vocabulary A word, its meaning and an example. Makes up to three cards. Cloze A sentence with blanks. Each blank becomes its own card. For a cloze, select the words to hide and press Ctrl Shift C , or wrap them yourself: The {{c1::hippocampus}} consolidates memory during {{c2::sleep}}. That makes two cards. Add a hint after a second pair of colons, like {{c1::sleep::stage}} , and it shows in place of the blank. Anything in the Extra field appears on the back of every card. Ctrl Enter saves the card and keeps the editor open with the same deck, type and tags, ready for the next one. Formulas and images Write LaTeX between dollar signs, like $E_k$ , or between double dollar signs for an equation on its own line. Each field holds up to three images: paste or drop them in. PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP all work, up to 20 MB each. Click an image during a review to zoom in. Your own card types Card types on a deck's menu opens the card type manager. A card type is a set of fields plus a front and a back template that use them, like {{Front}} . Card types are shared across your whole collection, and changing a template updates every card that uses it.

New makes a deck or a folder, and folders can nest. Drag a deck onto a folder to move it there. Click the icon beside a deck's name to give it an emoji. Open a deck to see its cards in a table, with search, filters for due, new, learning, suspended and flagged cards, and bulk actions for moving, tagging, suspending and deleting. Suspend takes a card out of every review without deleting it. Flag marks a card for whatever you like. Flagged cards get their own filter, and you can flag during a review. Search every card Browse cards at the top of the library lists every card in one table, and is the only place that searches across decks. Every word you type has to match, and words match as prefixes, so cell mem finds a card about the cell membrane. Right click a row to edit it, move it or open it in the side peek.
Study your cards, and let FSRS decide when you see each one again.

Study on a deck starts a review of the cards that are due. The menu next to it holds two practice modes that never touch your schedule. Review Shows the cards that are due. Every grade updates that card's schedule. Cram Runs through a deck's due cards, or all of them, without changing anything. Handy right before an exam. Test You type each answer, reveal it and grade yourself Missed, Close or Got it. The score screen compares with your last try and offers a retake of the ones you missed.

On a Mac, use Cmd for Ctrl . You can change all of these under Settings , then Keyboard . Space Reveal the answer, press again for Good 1 to 4 Again, Hard, Good, Easy E Edit the current card without leaving Ctrl Z Undo the last grade. Press again to step further back. Esc Leave the session In a test, Enter reveals and then marks Got it, and 1 2 3 pick Missed, Close or Got it.

Mnemo uses FSRS, the same open algorithm behind Anki. Each grade updates its guess of how well you know a card, and the card comes back just before you'd forget it. Again You didn't remember. Hard You got it, but slowly. Good You remembered. This is the normal one. Easy It was trivial. Each button shows when the card would come back. Grade honestly, because the schedule is only as good as your grades.

New cards go through a few short steps on the same day before they move to longer gaps. Again restarts the steps, Good moves on and Easy skips straight ahead. A card you forget later goes back through the steps to be relearned. A card you forget eight times is marked as a leech and tagged leech . That's usually a sign the card needs rewriting. You can also have leeches suspended automatically.

Each deck brings in up to 20 new cards a day and up to 200 reviews. Cards you're still learning are never cut off. If reviews start piling up, lower the new cards first, since every new card adds future reviews. The study day rolls over at 4 in the morning, not at midnight, so a late night session still counts for the day before. Missed a day? No problem, due cards simply wait for you.

Open Review settings from a deck's menu. Settings live in presets that several decks can share, so editing one changes every deck that uses it. New cards per day 20 by default Reviews per day 200 by default Desired retention How many reviews you aim to pass, from 80% to 97%. 90% by default. Higher means more reviews, lower means more forgetting. Learning steps The short steps for new cards, like 1m 10m Next day starts at 4 in the morning by default Lapse limit How many times a card can be forgotten before it counts as a leech. 8 by default. Fit FSRS to you Once a preset's decks have at least 400 reviews, press Optimize to tune FSRS to your own memory. If the result predicts your recall better, Apply puts it to work straight away. Use defaults goes back to the built in settings. Session options Shuffle card order mixes up the queue. Bury related cards holds back cards made from the same note until tomorrow, so three blanks from one sentence don't all show up at once. On by default. Auto reveal shows the answer after 5 or 10 seconds.
Bring your Anki decks, Markdown notes and Notion pages with you.

In Flashcards , press Import at the top of the library and drop in your .apkg file. Your cards come over with their fronts, backs, tags, clozes and images. So does your progress: due dates, intervals and review history all carry across, so a deck you've studied arrives studied. A deck called Spanish::Verbs becomes a Spanish folder with a Verbs deck inside. Mnemo uses the same FSRS scheduling as Anki and reads your memory data where Anki has it. Afterwards it tells you which cards came with that data. Cards without it settle in over their next few reviews. The same importer also takes CSV files with a front and a back column. Going back to Anki works too: export a deck as .apkg and it arrives studied.

In Notes , press Import notes at the top of the sidebar and pick a single file or a whole folder. To import straight into a folder you already have, right click it and choose Import notes here . Each note takes its title from the file name, so rename files first if the title matters. Headings, lists, to dos, quotes, code, tables and equations all come through.

In Notion, export your pages as Markdown & CSV . Run the export through our small Notion converter, which keeps your formatting intact, then bring the result in with Import notes like any other folder. You'll find the converter on our GitHub .

If an imported note, deck or map has the same name as one you have, choose what happens: Keep both adds a number to the new one, Skip leaves yours alone and Replace overwrites it. Replace always asks first.
Keep a copy of your library and get back what you deleted.

Go to Settings , then Storage & data , and press Back up . You get a single .mnemo-backup file with your notes, decks, maps, images, trash and settings. Sign ins and keys stay out of it. To restore, press Choose backup . Mnemo shows what's inside before it does anything, then restarts to finish. Your old data is kept aside for a while in case you change your mind.

Everything sits in one folder on your computer. Data folder , then Open takes you straight there. Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Mnemo macOS and Linux A Mnemo folder in your usual app data folder You can also back up by copying the whole folder. Close Mnemo first. To use a different folder, set MNEMO_DATA_DIR .

Right after you delete, an Undo button pops up. Missed it? Everything you delete stays in Settings , then Trash for 30 days. Press Restore to put it back where it was. Decks come back with their cards and review history intact. Delete for good and Empty trash remove things for real, and both ask first.
Themes, language, shortcuts and the rest of Settings.

Appearance Light, dark or match your system. You can also turn down motion. General The language: English, Deutsch, Español, Norsk or 日本語. Changes apply right away. Editor The width of the writing area, and autosave. Keyboard Rebind most shortcuts. Mnemo warns you if two clash. Notifications Turn off the popups. Messages still wait for you under the bell. Profile Your name, picture and colour. It never leaves your device.
Mnemo checks for updates on its own and lets you update now or later. You can check by hand and read the release notes under Settings , then Updates .
New features sometimes show up in English first. Spot a clumsy translation, or want to add your language? Translations live in the Mnemo repository , and help is always welcome.
Go from a fresh clone to a running development build.
The .NET 10 SDK. Node.js 24 with npm. Git, and on Linux or macOS also jq .

git clone https://github.com/onemnemo/mnemo.git cd mnemo/mnemo-web npm install cd .. Then fetch the bundled Typst binary. It's about 52 MB per platform, so it isn't committed. On Windows run ./scripts/restore-typst.ps1 , elsewhere ./scripts/restore-typst.sh . The build works without it, but PDF export from notes quietly stops working.

On Windows, dev.bat does everything for you. Everywhere else, start the host first: dotnet run --project Mnemo.Host -- --dev Then the web UI in a second terminal: cd mnemo-web npm run dev The order matters. In dev mode the host listens on 127.0.0.1:47210 and writes mnemo-web/.dev/api.json with the port and a fresh token. The Vite proxy reads that file and adds the token to every API call. Start Vite first and your API calls come back unauthorised until you restart it.

A development build uses the same data folder as an installed Mnemo. Point MNEMO_DATA_DIR at a scratch folder to keep them apart: MNEMO_DATA_DIR=/tmp/mnemo-dev dotnet run --project Mnemo.Host -- --dev

Every push to main and every pull request runs the same checks you can run locally. Run the half you touched before each push, and both before a pull request. dotnet test MnemoApp.sln Both xUnit projects, for Infrastructure and the Host npm run test The Vitest suite, run from mnemo-web npm run lint oxlint npx tsc -b Typechecking Test files sit next to the code they cover. Files that need a DOM opt in with a // @vitest-environment jsdom line at the top. Stuck on a build error? Search the existing issues first. If it looks new, open one with your OS, tool versions and the full error.
How the codebase is layered, how the UI talks to the backend and where data lives.

Mnemo is built as strict layers. Contracts point inward, implementations point outward, and nothing reaches across. Mnemo.Core Contracts: service interfaces, domain models and pure logic. Depends on almost nothing. Mnemo.Infrastructure Implements those contracts: SQLite storage, the FSRS scheduler, Markdown conversion, spellcheck, import and export. Mnemo.Host An ASP.NET Core minimal API on loopback, plus the native window. Wires up every service and exposes it under /api . mnemo-web The React and TypeScript app, built with Vite. Holds presentation state only. Business rules stay in C#. A change that spans layers lands in that order: the interface in Core, the implementation in Infrastructure, the endpoint in Host, and the screen in mnemo-web. Modules Features are modules that implement IModule , with hooks for services, translations, shortcuts, sidebar entries and widgets. They're found by reflection, so adding a feature never means editing a central list. Mnemo.Host/Composition/HostComposition.cs is where they get wired up.

The UI and the backend are one app on one machine. Kestrel binds to 127.0.0.1 only, and every request except the health check carries a bearer token made fresh at each launch. In production the host writes the token into the page it serves. In dev it goes through the Vite proxy. A strict content security policy with a nonce per launch blocks any script the app didn't ship, and connect-src 'self' keeps requests on the host. Push from server to client is one SSE stream at GET /api/events , used for things like toasts and shutdown. It never replays, so nothing should treat it as the source of truth. Closing the window doesn't kill a save halfway. The host sends a shutdown event, the UI gets a moment to flush, then the app closes. Pressing close twice skips the wait. Adding an endpoint Endpoints are minimal API handlers that live with their feature, like Mnemo.Host/Flashcards . Copy an existing feature folder: contract in, service call, DTO out, nothing clever in the handler.

Everything sits in one data folder, centred on a single SQLite file, mnemo.db , with images and attachments stored as files beside it. The database holds three shapes of data: A key value table of JSON documents behind IStorageProvider , for settings and most module state. A relational flashcard schema with an append only review log, in WAL mode with one writer. Note bodies, written with optimistic concurrency. A stale write gets a 409 with the stored version. Migrations run at startup, before the API takes its first request. Packages, backups and trash The .mnemo format is a zip with a manifest.json and a folder per module. Adding something exportable means writing a payload handler, not a new format. Markdown, CSV and Anki are adapters on top. A .mnemo-backup is a consistent snapshot of the whole profile. Restore is staged and swapped in on the next start, with the old data moved to restore-recovery first. Deleting leaves rows in place. Each module records the item in a shared trash ledger, kept for 30 days, and a background task sweeps expired entries.
How mnemo-web is organised, and the shared pieces every screen uses.

The UI is React and TypeScript, built with Vite. The notes editor is built on ProseMirror. Code is grouped by feature, in folders like src/notes , src/flashcards and src/settings , and talks to the host through a small typed fetch wrapper.

Style with the design tokens in src/styles/tokens.css . No hex colours or rgba() in component code. Icons come from the AppIcon wrapper, not straight from lucide. Popovers, dropdowns and menus use Radix. Never hand roll positioning. Server state goes through React Query. Every string a person can read is a translation key, through the useT() hook, in all five languages. oxlint is the floor, and the hook rules are errors, not warnings.

toast Reports what happened. Long work keeps one progress toast and updates it, instead of raising a second one. dialog.confirm and dialog.prompt Ask one question and wait for the answer. Questions queue rather than stack. Modal For anything with fields or more to look at. Handles focus, Escape and the backdrop for you. Popover A thin wrapper over Radix in src/components/ui/popover.tsx . Tooltips One shared tooltip that moves to whatever you hover. Stacking order lives in one place, src/lib/z-layers.ts . Use those tiers rather than inventing a z index. Overlays A file ending in Overlay is a convention, not a component. It decides whether a feature's surface is on screen at all, and gets mounted once in src/App.tsx beside the others.
From a first issue to a merged pull request.

Browse the issue tracker . The good first issue label is picked for newcomers. Comment on an issue before you start, so nobody does the same work twice. For big features, architecture changes or major UI work, open an issue first. Small fixes can go straight to a pull request.

The standard lives in the repository under standards/ , split by topic, and the repo always wins over this page. The rules reviewers catch most often: No em or en dashes anywhere a person can read: comments, commits, translations, release notes. No TODO , FIXME or HACK . Write the follow up into future-review/ instead. Every string a person can read is a translation key, in English, German, Spanish, Japanese and Norwegian. A performance number needs proof of correct output from the same run. On the .NET side, all I/O is async and cancellable, and .Result and .Wait() are banned.

Write type(scope): subject , lowercase and in the imperative: feat(notes): teach the sidebar tree to drag folders into folders fix(host): answer 409 with the stored version on stale note writes Types in use are feat , fix , perf , refactor , test and chore . A feature usually lands in two or three commits along its natural seams. Build and test before every commit, and never rewrite a commit that's already pushed. Sign off You keep your copyright, and contributions are under Apache 2.0. Sign each commit with git commit -s . That sign off is the only trailer a commit carries, so no co author or AI attribution lines.

Keep it to one concern, with no drive by reformatting. Say what changed and why, link the issue, and add screenshots for anything visual. Run the tests before you push. Review asks three things: does it solve a real problem, does it match the code around it, and does the app still behave honestly and predictably.
